steps.name: prompt
steps.text: Write a short introduction for a paper presenting a new dataset that separates factual accuracy from reasoning ability in language models. Explain the motivation, how this relates to truthfulness and honesty of AI systems, and briefly what the dataset is and what we found.

steps.name: skeleton_outline
steps.text:
- Goal: separate factual accuracy from reasoning ability
- Link to truthfulness and honesty; notion of belief
- The BaRDa dataset and findings

steps.name: detailed_outline
steps.text:
## Goal
- quantify factual accuracy and entailment reasoning of modern LMs
- existing benchmarks: HELM evaluation suite, EleutherAI LM evaluation harness, GPT4 Technical Report datasets
- factual accuracy and reasoning ability conflated in end-task evaluations
- want dataset separating the two
- approach: mixture of good and bad reasoning chains from correct and incorrect (counterfactual) statements

## Truthfulness and honesty
- measures indirectly capture "truthfulness" and "honesty" - critical if we depend on AI systems
- truthful: statements factually correct -> factual accuracy
- honest: "believes what it says" -> reporting correct implications of beliefs
- example: p = "birds can fly" -> "sparrows can fly", "eagles can fly" (modulo believing sparrows are birds)
- not confirming consequences (irrational) -> meaningless to say it "believes" p
- philosophy: believes p if it "acts as if p was true"

## BaRDa
- Belief and Reasoning Dataset: 9000 statements (some true), 3000 entailment-based reasoning steps (some valid)
- measure four GPT-series models
- clear progression for newer models; exception: GPT3 (text-davinci-003) stronger at entailment reasoning than GPT3.5 (gpt-3.5-turbo)
- offered to the community for existing and future models

Our goal is to better quantify the factual accuracy and also the entailment reasoning capabilities of modern language models. There are many evaluation benchmarks for testing models, e.g., the HELM evaluation suite, the EleutherAI LM evaluation harness, and the GPT4 Technical Report datasets, but factual accuracy and reasoning ability are often conflated in end-task evaluations. To deal with this limitation we want a dataset that separates these two notions more clearly. Our approach uses a mix of good and bad reasoning chains, which are built from a mix of correct and incorrect (counterfactual) statements about the world.

- the two measures indirectly capture "truthfulness" and "honesty" of an AI system; critical if we depend on such systems

- BaRDa: 9000 statements, 3000 entailment-based reasoning steps; four GPT-series models; clear progression, except GPT3 (text-davinci-003) beats GPT3.5 (gpt-3.5-turbo) at entailment reasoning; offered to the community

steps.name: rough_draft
steps.text:
Our goal is to better quantify the factual accuracy and also the entailment reasoning capabilities of modern language models. There are many evaluation benchmarks for testing models, e.g., the HELM evaluation suite, the EleutherAI LM evaluation harness, and the GPT4 Technical Report datasets, but factual accuracy and reasoning ability are often conflated in end-task evaluations. To deal with this limitation we want a dataset that separates these two notions more clearly. Our approach uses a mix of good and bad reasoning chains, which are built from a mix of correct and incorrect (counterfactual) statements about the world.

These two measures are useful in their own right, but they can also be seen as indirectly measuring the "truthfulness" and "honesty" of an AI system, which are critical properties to verify if we are going to depend on such systems. Using the definitions from prior work, an AI system is "truthful" if its statements are factually correct, so we can measure this just by measuring the factual accuracy of its statements. An "honest" AI system is one that "believes what it says", and we can operationalize this as reporting correct implications of its beliefs. For example, if a system says p = "birds can fly", then we would expect it to also say "sparrows can fly", "eagles can fly", etc. if it really believed p (modulo also believing sparrows are birds, etc.). On the other hand, if the system did not confirm these consequences (behaves irrationally), then it is somewhat meaningless to say the system "believes" p. This notion of belief is in line with work in philosophy, where an agent can be said to believe p if it "acts as if p was true".

To measure factual accuracy and reasoning accuracy we present BaRDa, a new Belief and Reasoning Dataset with 9000 statements, some true and some not, and 3000 entailment-based reasoning steps that use those statements, again some valid and some not. We first describe BaRDa, and then we use it to measure the belief and reasoning capabilities of four GPT-series models. We find a clear progression in both of these capabilities for newer models, with one exception: GPT3 (text-davinci-003) seems to be stronger at entailment reasoning than its successor GPT3.5 (gpt-3.5-turbo). We offer BaRDa to the community as a new evaluation tool to measure the performance of other models, both existing and future.

steps.name: revised_draft
steps.text:
Our goal is to better quantify both the factual accuracy and the entailment reasoning capabilities of modern language models. Although many evaluation benchmarks exist for testing models, e.g., the HELM evaluation suite [1], the EleutherAI LM evaluation harness [2], and the GPT4 Technical Report datasets [3], the notions of factual accuracy and reasoning ability are often conflated in end-task evaluations. To address this limitation, we aim for a dataset that separates these two notions more clearly. Our approach is to use a mixture of good and bad reasoning chains, constructed from a mixture of correct and incorrect (counterfactual) statements about the world.

Besides being useful in their own right, these two measures can be seen as indirectly measuring the “truthfulness” and “honesty” of an AI system, critical properties to verify if we are to depend on such systems. Using the definitions from [4], a “truthful” AI system is one whose statements are factually correct, so we can measure this simply by measuring the factual accuracy of its statements. Similarly, an “honest” AI system is one that “believes what it says” [4], which we can operationalize as reporting correct implications of its beliefs. For example, if a system says p = “birds can fly”, we would expect it to also say “sparrows can fly”, “eagles can fly”, etc. if it really believed p (modulo also believing sparrows are birds, etc.). Conversely, if the system did not confirm such consequences (behaves irrationally), it would be somewhat meaningless to say the system “believes” p. This notion of belief aligns with work in philosophy [5], where an agent can be said to believe p if it “acts as if p was true”.

To measure factual accuracy and reasoning accuracy, we present BaRDa, a new Belief and Reasoning Dataset consisting of 9000 statements, some true and some not, and 3000 entailment-based reasoning steps using those statements, again some valid and some not. We first describe BaRDa, then use it to measure the belief and reasoning capabilities of four GPT-series models. We find a clear progression in both capabilities for newer models, with the one exception that GPT3 (text-davinci-003) appears stronger at entailment reasoning than its successor GPT3.5 (gpt-3.5-turbo). We offer BaRDa to the community as a new evaluation tool for measuring the performance of other models, both existing and future.
